newsitem.title: ITALY: Zaire wants refugees out, slams Rwanda and Burundi.
newsitem.headline: Zaire wants refugees out, slams Rwanda and Burundi.

text.p: Zaire said on Thursday that aid for starving refugees in the east of the country should be sent to Rwanda and Burundi to encourage their return home and accused the world of "total indifference" to their fate.
Burundi said it agreed that its refugees should be encouraged to return but added that those guilty of massacres or genocide must be "separated" out.
It also called for an end to sanctions imposed against it, saying their lifting would help ensure the success of a multinational relief effort in eastern Zaire.

"There is a need to encourage the return of refugees to their original countries," Burundian Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira told Reuters in an interview at a five-day U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome.

"In the specific case of Burundi, there is no reason why these people could not return immediately," he said, adding that the estimated 150,000 Burundians in Zaire might pose some logistical problems but the country would be able to cope.

But he said "separating the authors of massacres and genocide which occurred in 1993 and 1994 in Burundi and Rwanda is a very important issue that should be taken into account" and criticised Zaire for its stance against his country.
"How can we help our refugees when Zaire is involved in economic sanctions against us?," he said, adding that dialogue between all countries in the region was needed.
Burundi's Tutsi-dominated military regime came to power on July 25 in a coup. Regional states including Tanzania, Kenya and Zaire imposed economic and political sanctions on Burundi six days later.
Zairean deputy prime minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda said it was up to Rwanda and Burundi to take back the ethnic Hutu refugees at risk from fighting in eastern Zaire.
He said "the fate of one million human beings is being played out amid the total indifference of the international community and of the governments (of Rwanda and Burundi)."

"...Zaire is launching a pressing appeal to the peoples of the world united on the occasion of this world summit on food security that all urgent action or all humanitarian aid destined for the refugees is delivered and distributed in their countries of origin, in Rwanda and Burundi and not in Zaire," he said.
Mutombo's speech reflected Zaire's position since the start of the crisis but U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien said in Kinshasa on Wednesday that the stance had changed.
"They (Zaire and Rwanda) agreed...to help the Rwandan, Burundian or Zairean refugees on the ground on Zairean territory," Chretien said.
He added that both countries saw the role of a Canadian-led force, including U.S. troops, to the area as to create the conditions for a voluntary return home of refugees.
Mutombo told Reuters that agreement had been given "on the condition that the force has a mission to evacuate...to maintain peace and help the refugees to return home".
He also expressed opposition to any dealings between aid agencies and Tutsi rebels who have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces bordering Rwanda in fighting since October 18.

"It is not in the interest of the refugees," Mutombo said when asked about efforts to bring aid to the city of Goma, where heavy fighting flared on Thursday between the rebels and their Hutu foes holed up in a teeming refugee camp.

Most of the refugees fled to Zaire from Rwanda in 1994 to escape a victorious Tutsi army which ended the killing by Hutus of some 800,000 Tutsis. The refugees, many of whom followed defeated Hutu soldiers out, fear reprisals if they go home.
